question: Given const [state, setState] = useState({ x: 1 }); setState({ x: 2 });, why might the old state.y disappear?
options: setState replaces the entire state object, not merging fields
useState always merges new state with old
setState is shallow-merged, y is preserved
Old fields are stored in prevState
explanation: Unlike this.setState in class components, useState's setState replaces the object entirely; you must manually merge: setState(prev => ({ ...prev, x: 2 })).

question: Why might useState with a complex initializer cause extra re-renders? const [state, setState] = useState(expensiveFunction());
options: expensiveFunction runs on every render, wasting computation
Use lazy initialization: useState(() => expensiveFunction()) runs once
expensiveFunction is cached, so it only runs during mount
useState never re-runs initializers after mount
explanation: Without a function, useState calls expensiveFunction on every render; wrapping it in a function (lazy init) runs it only once during mount.

question: Given multiple setState calls: setState(1); setState(2); setState(3);, what is the final state and when does it commit?
options: Final state is 3, all updates batched into single re-render
Three separate re-renders, one per setState
Final state is 1, later updates are ignored
Updates apply in reverse order: 3, 2, 1
explanation: React 18 batches all state updates in event handlers; all three setState calls merge and the component re-renders once with state = 3.

question: Why does this.state.x++ in a class component not update the component? this.state.x++;
options: Direct mutation doesn't trigger re-render; use setState instead
Mutation is valid but requires forceUpdate
Direct mutation works and updates the component automatically
Increment is synchronous but re-render is asynchronous
explanation: React doesn't detect mutations; setState notifies React to re-render, so mutating state directly is a silent bug (no update happens).

question: Given const [items, setItems] = useState([1, 2, 3]); items.push(4);, why doesn't the component update?
options: Array mutation is not detected by React; use immutable patterns
push is synchronous, update is asynchronous
React tracks mutations automatically
push returns undefined, state is not updated
explanation: Mutating state arrays doesn't trigger re-renders; create a new array: setItems([...items, 4]) or setItems(items.concat(4)).

question: Why might sharing state between siblings require lifting state to the parent? Why is this inefficient for deeply nested components?
options: Parent re-renders all descendants when state changes, even unrelated ones
State can be shared without lifting, no performance cost
Siblings cannot share state at all
Lifting state is always the optimal solution
explanation: Lifting state to a parent causes the parent and all children to re-render when state changes; deeply nested trees waste renders on unrelated components.

question: Given const [x, setX] = useState(0); setTimeout(() => setX(x + 1), 1000);, why might x be stale after multiple calls?
options: setTimeout captures the current x, calling setX(x + 1) is stale
Use setX(prev => prev + 1) to avoid stale closure
x is updated before setTimeout executes
This pattern is safe and will always increment by 1
explanation: setTimeout captures x in a closure; if called multiple times, each timeout uses the x from when it was scheduled, not the current value.

question: Why might storing props in state cause sync issues? const [localProp, setLocalProp] = useState(props.data);
options: State is set once at mount; prop changes don't update state
State and props auto-sync in React
Storing props in state is safe and recommended
Only derived state should be stored
explanation: State is initialized with props.data at mount; if props.data changes later, state stays the same, causing drift (use props directly or sync with useEffect).

question: Given const [state, setState] = useState(null); setState(undefined);, what is the state after setState?
options: State becomes undefined, update commits normally
setState ignores undefined, state stays null
Setting to undefined is not allowed
State becomes null, undefined is coerced
explanation: setState(undefined) is valid and updates state to undefined; only skipped if setState's argument is exactly the same reference as current state.

question: Why is const [state, setState] = useState(() => ...) different from const [state, setState] = useState(...)? When should each be used?
options: Lazy init runs only once, eager init runs every render
Both run once, lazy is just syntax sugar
Lazy init runs on every render, eager init runs once
Lazy init is slower than eager init
explanation: Lazy init (function) runs only during mount; eager init (value) runs on every render even if unused, wasting computation for expensive operations.
